title: Skeuomorphism vs Neomorphism
lede: Both make surfaces feel physical, and both are usually filed under "fake 3D". They get there by opposite means: one draws material, the other only lights it.
verdict: Skeuomorphism paints the material — paper gradients, stitched dashed borders, an element that is a different colour from the page. Neomorphism paints nothing: the card is the same colour as the background, and two paired shadows are the only thing that makes it exist.
brief: The confusion is fair. Neither style uses flat colour blocks, both lean on shadow, and both are associated with the same era of interface design. From a screenshot at 50 percent they can look like the same idea.

The difference shows up in one question: what colour is the card? A skeuomorphic card here is a warm paper tone sitting on a darker leather ground, with a 1px solid #2c1d10 outline and a dashed #c4b49a line inset from the edge standing in for stitching. A neomorphic card is #e0e0e0 on an #e0e0e0 page with border: none — it has no outline at all, so the only thing separating it from the background is a light shadow on one corner and a dark one on the other.

whenA: The interface is meant to feel like an object — a notebook, a mixing desk, a till — and the material is part of the metaphor
There is very little content per screen, so the texture has room and does not compete with text
The audience is not design-literate and responds to recognisable physical cues rather than to typographic hierarchy
whenB: You want a soft, quiet surface without textures, and the page carries one idea at a time
Every element is a control — buttons, toggles, sliders — where the pressed state can carry the entire interaction language
You can afford to keep the palette to a single value, which is the condition the style depends on
promptDelta: The sentence that decides it is whether the element is a different colour from the page. Say that the card is a warmer tone than the ground with a 1px dark outline and a dashed stitch line, and you get skeuomorphism. Say the card is the same value as the page, has no border, and is shaped only by a light shadow on one side and a dark one on the other, and you get neomorphism. A model asked for "soft 3D" without that clause will produce a drop shadow on a white card, which is neither.
